description: The Saharan frog is the park's true water-specialist, living in the gueltas, springs and irrigation channels fed by the winter rains. Croaking males gather at the water from winter into spring, and the tadpoles must develop fast before the heat returns.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The banded orb-weaver spins its wide, zigzag-streaked web low among grass and shrubs across the park, the silver-banded female far larger than the male. Grasshoppers and flies that blunder in are wrapped in silk and eaten at the web's centre.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: A pale grey raptor with black shoulders and burning red eyes, the black-winged kite hunts rodents by hovering over open ground — exactly the technique it uses on the grazed plain of Bouhedma, where a breeding pair was recorded in February 2013.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A slim grey hawk of acacia woodland with finely barred underparts and long yellow legs. It hunts lizards and insects from a low perch and gives a piping, melodic song at first light.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A small, slender brown eagle that breeds in sub-Saharan Africa and migrates north with the European summer. It soars over open woodland on narrow, long wings while searching for birds and small mammals.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A large, dark eagle with a pale golden nape and white shoulder patches in the adult. It hunts medium-sized mammals from a soaring flight and nests in tall trees or on pylons.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A small white vulture with a black flight line, a wedge-shaped tail and a featherless yellow face. It feeds on carrion and offal and is one of the few birds known to use stones as tools to break eggs.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: One of the heaviest flying birds in the world, uniformly dark brown with a huge flat profile in the air. It patrols open hillsides for large carcasses, often feeding alongside griffon vultures.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A sandy, long-necked vulture with a white ruff that wheels over cliffs and ridges in small groups. It locates carcasses by sight and feeds in a scrum at the ground.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A dark, broad-winged eagle of wetlands and forest edges, spotted with pale buff on the upperwing of the young bird. It quarters marshes for frogs, small birds and rodents.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A dark brown eagle with a long, square tail and a gape that reaches back past the eye. It breeds on the open steppe and migrates in large numbers, resting on the ground and on pylons.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A small, gentle-faced kestrel that nests colonially in holes in walls, cliffs and buildings. Males are chestnut with an unbarred blue-grey wing, and the whole family feeds almost entirely on insects.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A medium-sized eagle of the cliffs, dark above and pale below with a dark leading edge to the wing. It hunts partridges and hares over the plain, and the pair stays on its territory all year.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The kestrel hangs motionless in the air over the road verges, tail fanned, watching for mice and lizards. It nests in a cliff niche or a cavity and can be seen hunting from first light.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The largest owl of the park — ear tufts, orange eyes — hunting rats and hares from a rock or an acacia after dark. Its deep call carries over the plain on still nights.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A small, flat-headed owl that hunts by day as well as at dusk, perching on a stone or a post. It lives in the cavities of old walls and hunts beetles and mice on the bare ground.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The North African ostrich was reintroduced to Bouhedma after a century of absence, and now roams the open plain in loose flocks. In the breeding season males turn brick-red on the neck and shins, and can outrun any predator in the park.
source_reference: Park reintroduction & management records

description: A plump, cryptic bird of steppe grassland; the male has a striking black-and-white neck pattern in summer and makes a short, sharp two-note call. It creeps through crops and stubble.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A sandy, pigeon-like desert bird with a yellow-bordered crown and a rounded head. Males carry water to their chicks soaked into specially adapted belly feathers.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A big, grey pigeon with a white neck crescent and white wing bars, the largest pigeon in Europe. It feeds on the ground in woods, orchards and parkland.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A pale sandy dove with a narrow black half-collar on the back of the neck and a soft, three-syllable coo. A famous coloniser, it spread from Asia across Europe in the 20th century.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: The partridge of the rocky slopes: grey head, black eye-stripe and chestnut flank bars. It runs uphill at the first alarm, and the covey gathers on the open patches at dusk.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A pigeon-like bird of the open sand, sandy above and warm orange below. The males carry water to the chicks in specially structured belly feathers, flying in to the water point every evening.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The wild pigeon of cliffs and ruins from which the domestic pigeon descends: blue-grey with two black wing-bars. Feral flocks from the old farms also feed on the plain beside the wood pigeons.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A sooty black songbird with a bright orange tail that it shivers as it stands on a wall or rooftop. Originally a mountain species, it has become a thoroughly urban bird across Europe.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A familiar all-black thrush with an orange bill and eye-ring; the female is brown and streaked. The male sings a mellow, fluted song from high perches, often long after dark.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A pale, sandy finch with a thick, stubby bill that trumpets a nasal, metallic call in flocks. A bird of hot, bare desert, it turns up around villages and fields in the dry season.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A tame, grey-brown bunting of North African villages that feeds around doorways and marketplaces, often nesting in walls. Its dry, rattling call is a sound of every southern town.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A streaked brown lark with a tall pointed crest, singing from a bush or a wire rather than in the air. It lives close to people and livestock and nests in a scrape under a stone.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The lark of the rocks and the cultivation edges, almost identical to the crested lark but with a shorter, squared crest and heavier streaking on the breast. Its song is shorter and less musical.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A plain, sand-coloured lark of the bare rocky hills, so close in tone to the ground that it is found first by movement. It sings from a low stone and keeps to the empty slopes.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A black wheatear with a white rump, hopping between the rocks and the old walls of the jebel. The male carries small stones to the nest hole as a display, and the pair defends a cliff territory all year.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A pale wheatear of the open sand; the male has a black throat and black ear-coverts. It hunts insects on the ground with short runs, tail cocked, and sings from a small bush after the heat.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A small, dark stork of the African grasslands, white below with grey legs and a red bill base. It follows rains and insects, and was recorded in Tunisia for the first time in 2022.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A mottled dark-brown dabbling duck with an olive-yellow bill, the American black duck of eastern North America. A male stayed more than two weeks at the Oued Beja wetland from 25 June to 8 July 2020 - the first record for Tunisia and for North Africa. Ouni et al. 2024 publishes it as «Canard noir» with Anas rubripes as the scientific name.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A tiny, round waterbird with a steep forehead and a stubby tail that seems to have none. It dives for fish and insects and disappears among reeds at the slightest disturbance.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: A heavy, streaked heron that lives hidden in reedbeds, where its buff-and-brown plumage matches the dead stems. The male inflates its throat and booms across the marsh at night.
source_reference: Ouni et al. 2024 — Alauda 92(2)

description: The maidenhair fern hides in the shadiest, wettest corners of Djebel Bouhedma, clinging to dripping limestone walls beside springs and seepages. Its fan-shaped leaflets on fine black stalks are unmistakable, and it dies back in summer to return with the first winter rains.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Buffel grass grows in dense blue-green tussocks across the park's grazing plains and is one of the two most frequent species of the survey. Its bristly seed heads travel in the fur of passing animals, and the tussocks are prized fodder for flock and gazelle alike.
source_reference: Rouissi et al. 2024 — Caldasia 46(1)

description: Alfa grass builds the open, pale-green tufts of the Bouhedma steppe: the esparto that has been cut for paper, cordage and basketry for centuries. It is the signature plant of the park's grasslands, the third most frequent species of the survey, and vulnerable on the Red List.
source_reference: Rouissi et al. 2024 — Caldasia 46(1)

description: A low perennial grass whose knotted base gives it its name, nodose finger-grass spreads in the open ground between the shrubs of the park. Its finger-like spikes release seed through the hot months, and the young growth is grazed by livestock and by dorcas gazelles.
source_reference: Rouissi et al. 2024 — Caldasia 46(1)

description: A feathered desert grass whose twice-branched awns catch the light, obtuse two-awn is the winter fodder of the park's rangeland. The tufts hold the fine sand in place, and the seed walks into the soil as the awns twist with the humidity of the night.
source_reference: Rouissi et al. 2024 — Caldasia 46(1)

description: Fringed two-awn is the tall, shimmering grass of the park's moving sands, its long ciliated awns glowing at sunrise. The deep root system binds the dune edges that the corridor vegetation holds against the wind.
source_reference: Rouissi et al. 2024 — Caldasia 46(1)

description: A grey, rush-like grass of the clay plains, tougher than alfa and once gathered for the same paper and cordage. It forms dense tufts that hold the soil after the first autumn rain.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A stiff desert grass with sharp pointed leaves that gives the sand its first hold. Its feathery seed heads drift into small dunes around the bushes of the southern plain.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: Broomrapes are parasites with no chlorophyll at all — pale, scaly spikes that push up beside the roots of the plants they feed on. The tribe includes several species that attack crops and native shrubs across the drylands around the park.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: White broom is a deep-rooted, almost leafless shrub that stabilises the moving sand of Bouhedma's southern plain. After winter rain it erupts in small white pea-flowers, and its root network binds the dunes against the sirocco.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: Silk vine is a climbing, milky-sapped shrub woven through the acacia scrub of the park. Its narrow leaves and silky seed pods make it easy to recognise, and it has long been used in traditional medicine for digestive complaints.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: White wormwood perfumes the stony plains of Bouhedma with bitter, silvery foliage. It is one of the most grazing-resistant plants of the steppe, and a traditional remedy for colic and fever across the Maghreb.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: A leafless, salt-tolerant shrub whose green, jointed stems do the photosynthesis, the broom hammad is among the most frequent plants of the Borj BouHedma area in the park's phytoecological survey. It holds the sandy soil together after grazing.
source_reference: Rouissi et al. 2024 — Caldasia 46(1)

description: A grey-green subshrub that turns the stony hillsides violet in spring, shrubby moricandia is one of the most frequent plants of the Borj BouHedma relevés. Its glaucous leaves reflect the sun and its deep woody base survives both drought and grazing.
source_reference: Rouissi et al. 2024 — Caldasia 46(1)

description: Schmitt's hammad is a compact, salt-excreting dwarf shrub of the stony steppe, as frequent as the broom hammad in the Borj BouHedma area. Its jointed stems store water and its small wind-pollinated flowers appear after the spring rain.
source_reference: Rouissi et al. 2024 — Caldasia 46(1)

description: A succulent subshrub of the plateaux, mountain anabasis carries its leaves as tiny scales on fleshy jointed stems that store water. It thrives on the gypsum soils of the park's higher ground and is one of the most frequent species recorded around Borj BouHedma.
source_reference: Rouissi et al. 2024 — Caldasia 46(1)

description: A woody, salt-loving subshrub of the hamada edges, salt gymnocarpos carries small fleshy leaves that store water through the long dry season. Livestock browse it, and the survey ranked it among the most frequent plants around Borj BouHedma.
source_reference: Rouissi et al. 2024 — Caldasia 46(1)

description: Rhanterium is a low, aromatic shrub of the Tunisian steppe and one of the defining plants of the rangelands around Bouhedma. After the winter rain it covers the stony plain with a haze of small yellow flower heads, and its roots hold the thin soil against wind and grazing.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: A small sumac of the dry hills whose leaves are divided into three leaflets and turn red in autumn. Its red fruit clusters feed thrushes, and its roots bind the loose soil of the slopes.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A thorny, rounded shrub of the steppe with glossy three-veined leaves and small yellow flowers. Its tiny apple-like fruits feed birds and rodents, and goats browse it where nothing else stays green.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A low, aromatic sub-shrub of the open sand, silver-grey and resinous. It scent the steppe after rain, and hares and gazelles browse its young shoots.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A yellow-flowered legume of the Saharan sands with silky hairs all over its pods. Like the rest of the bean family it fixes nitrogen and enriches the poor soil around it.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A spiny, cushion-shaped milk-vetch that grows as a low dome against the wind. The yellow pea flowers open inside the thorns, and the inflated pods dry into rattling balls.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A small evergreen shrub of the saline sands whose tiny leaves are covered in white hairs, giving the whole bush a silver cast. It flowers in the middle of winter, when little else is open.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A grey, mealy saltbush that takes salt into its leaves and sheds it on the surface. Gazelles and Barbary sheep browse it, and it stays green after the grasses have burnt off.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A woody saltwort of the gypseous plains, winter-green and much grazed after rain. It is one of the shrubs that hold the crust of the plain together against the sirocco.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A low, fleshy-leaved shrub of the salt flats, white-flowered in the summer. It grows where little else can, at the edge of the chotts, and its roots follow the water table down.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A thorny cushion shrub of the saline sands with notched leaves and small black fruits that mice and birds carry off. Its ashes were once boiled for salt.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A leafless desert shrub whose green, twisted stems do the work of leaves. It survives the dry season by shedding everything else, and camels and goats browse it on the open plain.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The caper bush of the old walls and the rocky slopes, with white flowers that open for a single day and buds pickled as the spice of the same name. It roots in the mortar of ruined buildings.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The umbrella thorn acacia is the signature tree of Bouhedma's pre-Saharan savanna. Its flat, parasol-shaped crown fixes nitrogen in poor soils, and its long seed pods feed oryx, gazelles and Barbary sheep right through the dry season.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: Phoenician juniper holds the upper slopes of Djebel Bouhedma, forming open woodland with wild olive and Atlas pistachio. Individual trees may stand for several centuries, tolerating frost, drought and the thinnest limestone soils.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The wild olive is a hardy relic of Mediterranean woodland surviving on the rocky terraces of Djebel Bouhedma. Its small bitter drupes feed birds and rodents, while its twisted, hollowing trunk records centuries of fire and browsing.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: Atlas pistachio is a slow, aromatic tree of the park's stony hillsides, valued by wildlife for its resin-rich nuts. Its foliage burns red in autumn, and its resin has been collected by local communities for centuries.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The umbrella thorn is the classic acacia of the North African deserts, its flat crown spread wide to capture every drop of the rare rain. Twisted paired spines and white pom-pom flowers set it apart from the park's other acacias, and its twisted pods are prime dry-season fodder for oryx, gazelles and Barbary sheep.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The desert pancratium waits for the autumn rain buried in the sand, then puts up a strap of leaves and a cluster of white, fragrant trumpets that last a few nights. It flowers across the open plain of the park, where the survey found it in almost a fifth of the relevés.
source_reference: Rouissi et al. 2024 — Caldasia 46(1)

description: A low grey subshrub covered in yellow flowers that open only in the sun, the Cairo rockrose carpets the gypseous ground of the park in spring. Its hairy leaves hold a film of humidity against the dry wind of the plain.
source_reference: Rouissi et al. 2024 — Caldasia 46(1)

description: Sea lavender earns its name from the lilac sprays that appear on salty ground after the spring rains. Its wiry, almost leafless stems and salt-tolerant roots let it thrive on the gypseous and saline soils where most plants cannot, dotting the flats with pale colour.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The antlion's larva is the pit-digger of the park's sheltered sand: it buries itself in fine drifts, waits at the bottom of its conical trap and pulls down ants that stumble in. The adult is a delicate, lacewing-like flier of summer nights.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Feral honey bees work Bouhedma's spring bloom, from thyme and wormwood to the acacia canopy, and store honey in hollow trunks and rock cavities. Their pollination keeps the park's plant community reproducing year after year.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: Desert ants sprint across open sand at midday, when predators are beaten by the heat, to scavenge insects that have died of sunstroke. They navigate by counting their steps and reading the polarised pattern of the sky.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: Harvester ants cut and carry grass seeds to granaries beneath their nests, wearing trails across the plain. Their seed stores feed rodents and birds, and the spoil heaps enrich the soil in a wide ring around each nest.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The sacred scarab rolls balls of livestock dung across Bouhedma's grazed plains, burying them as food for its larvae. Its serrated forelegs and glossy black body are built for cutting, rolling and digging.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: Darkling beetles walk the sand between shrubs, feeding on plant debris and ranking among the steppe's main recyclers. Their fused wing-cases seal in moisture, so they never need to drink in the driest months.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: This small scarab beetle, dusted with white spots, feeds on pollen and petals and is one of the key flower visitors of the spring steppe. It clusters on yellow composites a few days after the rains.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: Pimelia is a round, matte-black darkling beetle that walks the park's sands at dawn and dusk, its fused wing cases a shield against the dry air. Like many desert beetles it lives on wind-blown plant debris and whatever the desert provides.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Phyllognathus excavatus is a small scarab beetle of sandy ground, one of the many dung beetles that keep the park's plains clean by burying livestock and wild herbivore droppings. Males carry a small horn on the head that gives the genus its name.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Eugaster spinulosa is a heavy, slow bush-cricket of the North African scrub, its spiny hind legs and strong mandibles making it one of the more formidable plant-eating insects of the park. Males call from the ground through the warm months.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The Barbary bush cricket lives on the ground among the low scrub of the Tunisian drylands, its long antennae and robust body typical of the barrel-bellied bush-crickets. It is active from spring into autumn and is a regular find on student surveys.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The Old World swallowtail is Bouhedma's largest butterfly, patrolling the wadi edges in spring in search of fennel and rue on which to lay. Its yellow, black-veined wings trail elegant blue-and-red eyespots near the tails.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The convolvulus hawk-moth hovers like a hummingbird to sip nectar from deep flowers at dusk, its long tongue reaching where no other insect can. Its grey-and-pink forewings camouflage it flat against bark during the day.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The spurge hawk-moth flies from March to June, its pink-and-olive hindwings flashing as it feeds on evening flowers. Its caterpillars strip the toxic spurge that colonises the park's disturbed ground, storing the poison for their own defence.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: An erebid moth of the park's dry scrub, Gnamptonyx innexa flies at night and rests by day among dry grass where its grey-brown wings make it almost invisible. Students recorded it during the park's night surveys.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: A striking erebid moth whose forewings carry bold black and cream bands over olive-brown, with metallic eyespots on the hindwings. It is a strong migrant, common across North Africa, and turns up in the park's light traps through the warm months.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The beet armyworm is a small, restless moth known mainly as an agricultural pest, whose caterpillars strip the leaves of a wide range of crops and wild plants. The adults migrate in numbers and are regular visitors to the park's light traps.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Caddisflies are the park's quiet water-indicator: their aquatic larvae build cases of sand grains or plant debris in the springs and channels of Djebel Bouhedma, and the winged adults gather on the vegetation beside the water at dusk.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The Saharan bluet is a small damselfly of North Africa's standing water, males flashing pale blue over black as they patrol the reeds. It breeds wherever water holds through the year, and is one of the region's characteristic odonates.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The epaulet skimmer is a bold, sun-loving dragonfly of rocky desert streams, perching on warm stones and chasing rivals along the park's watercourses. Mature males turn powder-blue, and the pale 'epaulet' stripe on the thorax gives the species its name.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The violet dropwing is one of the most vivid dragonflies of the Sahara's edges, males glowing violet-red as they perch on the tip of any dry twig above the water. It spreads north with the heat and is now common along Bouhedma's springs.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: This long-headed grasshopper is built for the park's dry grasslands: a pointed, cone-shaped head, a slender green or straw-coloured body and powerful hind legs for escaping over open ground. Its call is a faint crackling rattle carried on the wind.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Ochrilidia is a genus of small, slender grasshoppers of the Saharan steppe, easily overlooked until they fly a short distance and settle again on bare ground. Like many desert grasshoppers they time their breeding to the right rains.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Geotomini is a tribe of broad-winged, ground-dwelling grasshoppers of arid lands, recorded by the park's students on the stony plains of Bouhedma. Most identification stops at the tribe, since separating the genera needs close examination.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The praying mantis stands motionless among the park's tall herbs and shrubs, its spiked forelegs ready to snatch whatever passes. The foamy egg-case it glues to dry stems in autumn shelters the next generation through the cold months.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Unlike its tree-dwelling relatives, this mantis hunts on bare ground, sprinting across sand and stone after small prey with surprising speed. Its flattened, sand-coloured body and shortened wings let it hide in plain sight on the desert pavement of the park's southern plain.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: Kuhl's pipistrelle hunts low over the wadi and the two basins of Bouhedma, snapping up midges and mosquitoes on the wing. It was one of the three bats most often recorded in the park's year-long survey, and by day it sleeps in rock crevices and in the walls of the old farm buildings.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: The common pipistrelle is the small bat of the park's open country, quartering the acacia stand and the edge of the steppe a few metres above the ground. In Bouhedma it was recorded from April to October and taken in the mist nets set across the water holes.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: The meridional serotine replaced the northern serotine across North Africa, and it is the bat captured most often in Bouhedma — the largest catches of the survey. A powerful, deliberate flier, it feeds above the plain and the acacia forest and roosts in walls and rock fissures.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: A bat of caves and deep crevices, the bent-wing bat lives in colonies and commutes a long way from its roost to hunt over the wadi. In the park's survey it was the third most abundant species, peaking in late spring when the insects hatch.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: The free-tailed bat flies high and fast above the park, its tail projecting well beyond the membrane like a rudder. It was recorded along the Bou Hedma wadi — its preferred habitat in the survey — taking beetles and moths on the wing.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: A long-eared bat whose range reaches southern Tunisia, Gaisler's listens with enormous ears for the rustle of an insect on a leaf, then takes it without a chase. It is a quiet flier along the hedges, walls and rock faces of the park after dark.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: A mouse-eared bat of the Maghreb and the Mediterranean islands, recorded in Bouhedma but rarely — the survey netted it on a few nights only. It hunts around water and rock faces on small moths and flies, and is still listed as data deficient on the Red List.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: The desert long-eared bat waits on a rock or a branch and grabs scorpions, spiders and beetles with its feet — it is unhurt by the sting of the park's own fat-tailed scorpion. It works along the wadi, which the survey found to be its preferred habitat here.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: The mouse-tailed bat has a tail as long as its body, left hanging clear of the membrane. A Saharan species at the northern edge of its range, it drinks on the wing over the basins of Bouhedma and roosts in the warm crevices of cliffs and ruins.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: Named for the horseshoe of skin around its nose, this is the Mediterranean counterpart of the greater horseshoe bat. In Bouhedma it was recorded rarely, close to the cliffs and rock shelters where it spends the day — the Red List calls it near threatened.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: The largest horseshoe bat of the park, it flies slowly through the acacia woodland reading the world with a beam of sound cast from the nose-leaf. Bouhedma lies at the southern edge of its range, and the species was recorded rarely in the survey.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: The smallest horseshoe bat of Bouhedma, light enough for the fine mist net strung over the wadi. It is a constant, fluttering flier, hunting along the edges of the vegetation after dark with its nose-leaf working like a megaphone.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: Mehely's horseshoe bat is a North African species of gorges and rock shelters, assessed as vulnerable. A few individuals were recorded in Bouhedma, where the park's cliffs offer the warm crevices the species depends on for its day roosts.
source_reference: Dalhoumi et al. 2016 — Turkish J. Zool. 40(6)

description: A small insect-eating bat of the cliffs and old walls whose nose-leaf ends in three points. It roosts in the cool caves of the jebel and hunts beetles and moths over the oueds after dusk.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A fast, long-winged bat of tomb walls and rock fissures, recognisable by the bare skin at the base of the tail. It hunts high above the plain in long straight passes.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A small pipistrelle of warm, dry country, gleaning insects from leaves close to walls, trees and rocks. It roosts in crevices and is taken in the nets set at the park's water points.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A bat of open country and short grass that flies high over the steppe after the last light. In Bouhedma it is recorded from spring to autumn, feeding on the small flies rising from the grazing grounds.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A big-eared bat with a deep slit down the face, flying low and slow across the plain to pick beetles and scorpions off the ground. It roosts in burrows and buildings and hangs in a distinctive head-down pose.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: Tunisia has no jackal: its canid is the African golden wolf, a separate species only recognised in 2015 and long filed under the golden jackal. Bouhedma's wolves hunt hares and rodents at dusk, scavenge behind the herds of oryx and gazelle, and answer each other with howling at first light.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The red fox occupies the wooded slopes of Djebel Bouhedma, digging its den among rocks and hunting rodents at night. It is a comparatively recent coloniser of the park's higher, cooler zones, where it shares the djebel with caracal and Barbary sheep.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: Shy and almost entirely nocturnal, the striped hyena ranges the rocky fringes of the park in search of carrion. Its sloping back, bristling mane and black-on-cream stripes make it unmistakable on camera-trap nights, though few visitors ever see one.
source_reference: Park reintroduction & management records

description: The caracal is the secretive cat of the rocky edges: a short red coat, black ear tufts and a look that disappears against the stone. It springs on hares and bustards from cover, so it needs scrub and silence more than open ground.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The ancestor of the domestic cat, slightly larger and longer-legged, with faint banding on the forelegs. It lives alone on the plain and in the acacia thickets, hunting rodents and gerbils at night.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A small, pale desert fox with very large ears that lose heat quickly. It keeps away from people, hunting insects and gerbils on the sand flats after dark and digging its burrow in open ground.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The longest mongoose of the region: a dark grizzled animal with a black-tipped tail that hunts in pairs along the oueds and the reeds. It takes birds, snakes and eggs, and is rarely seen away from cover.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The genet is a slender, spotted climber, closer to a civet than to a cat. It slips through the acacia at night hunting insects and small birds, and rests by day in a hollow tree or a rock crevice.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The white-faced hedgehog of orchards and scrub, smaller than the European species, with ears that show above the spines. It walks long distances at night for beetles, snails and scorpions.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A small, dark-faced hedgehog of the rocky desert with big ears and a bare-skinned flank line. It is most active after midnight, moving between shrubs and drinking at the water points the park keeps open.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: Declared extinct in the wild in 2000, the scimitar oryx was reintroduced to Bouhedma and now browses the acacia plains in small herds. Its long, backwards-curving horns and white coat with a russet neck are unmistakable against the sand.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The dama gazelle is the largest of the gazelles and one of Bouhedma's reintroduced stars, released here from captive Mhorr stock. Its white rump and dark russet neck make a bold two-tone silhouette on the open plain.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The small dorcas gazelle can live its whole life without drinking, taking moisture from leaves and green pods. It moves in pairs and family groups across the plain, always alert, and can sprint at 80 km/h to escape a closing golden wolf.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The Barbary sheep, or aoudad, keeps to the cliffs and gorges of Djebel Bouhedma, coming down to the plain at night to feed. Its hanging chest fringe and heavy, backward-curving horns identify adult rams from a distance.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: Gundis are compact rock rodents that press themselves flat against warm stone to absorb heat at midday. They live in family parties inside the crevices of Djebel Bouhedma, feeding on leaves, seeds and flower petals.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: A pale, long-tailed gerbil of stony desert, named after the Tarabulus region of Libya. In the park's survey it selected plots that had been grazed, where the soil is loose enough for its burrows.
source_reference: Traba et al. 2016 — J. Arid Environ. 131

description: A small, sandy gerbil with large eyes and a tufted tail tip, common on fine sand. It digs deep burrow systems and forages at night for seeds and the occasional insect.
source_reference: Traba et al. 2016 — J. Arid Environ. 131

description: A small gerbil of sandy habitats, formerly confused with the Baluchistan gerbil under the name Gerbillus nanus. It prefers open, well-drained ground with sparse cover.
source_reference: Traba et al. 2016 — J. Arid Environ. 131

description: The largest of the park's gerbils, a long-legged rodent of firm, disaggregated soil. The survey found it using the barest, most open ground of all six species studied.
source_reference: Traba et al. 2016 — J. Arid Environ. 131

description: A robust, buff-brown jird with a tufted tail, living in colonies of deep burrows in sand. It stores seeds in chambered granaries and rarely drinks, taking its water from food.
source_reference: Traba et al. 2016 — J. Arid Environ. 131

description: A large, powerful jird, the biggest murid of the North African desert, with a black-tufted tail. Aggressive and omnivorous, it takes seeds, insects and even small vertebrates.
source_reference: Traba et al. 2016 — J. Arid Environ. 131

description: The largest rodent of the park, weighing up to 12 kg, with a crest of long bristles and black-and-white quills that reach 30 cm. It gnaws bones for minerals and spends the day in a burrow on the jebel.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A hopping desert rodent with a kangaroo's proportions — long hind legs, a tufted tail and almost invisible ears. It leaves star-shaped tracks around the bushes at night and never comes out in daylight.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A plump gerbil-like rodent of the saline soils that takes all its water from the succulent plants it eats. It digs its burrow at the foot of the halophytes and works the cool hours.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: Leeches are recorded from the park's permanent waters, where they attach to frogs and water birds and move with looping, swimming strokes. Their presence shows how much life the small springs of Bouhedma support beyond the familiar headline species.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The sandfish skink dives into loose sand as if swimming, leaving only a wiggle trail behind it. Its polished, wedge-shaped head and countersunk scales let it pass through grains with almost no drag.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The ocellated skink is the commonest lizard on Bouhedma's stony ground, its bronze body freckled with black-and-white eye-spots. It basks on warm stone and bolts into a crevice at the first shadow of a passing bird.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: Bosk's fringed lizard runs so fast over hot sand that its fringed toes spread like tiny snowshoes. Males flash a black-and-white throat fan while defending a sunlit boulder from rivals.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The Moorish gecko is the familiar wall gecko of North African courtyards, its tubercled skin and wide toe pads letting it cling to any surface. It hunts insects around lights after dusk and calls softly in spring to defend its stretch of wall.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The largest lizard of the park — up to a metre and a half — with a long forked tongue and a powerful tail. It digs out rodent burrows and takes eggs, and disappears down the sand at the first footstep.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A heavy, flattened lizard with a ring of hard spines on the tail, basking on the rock faces at midday. It feeds on the flowers and leaves of the desert shrubs and retreats into a deep burrow.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A slow, three-toed climber that catches insects with a tongue fired in a fraction of a second. It changes colour with light, temperature and mood, and the female buries her eggs in the sand of the plain.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A rock-dwelling agama whose males turn orange-red on the head during the breeding season. It basts on the stones of the jebel, waving its head to defend a territory of a few square metres.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The deathstalker hides under stones by day and hunts small invertebrates at night. Its sting is among the most potent of any scorpion, yet its pale yellow body makes it almost invisible on the park's limestone.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The fat-tailed scorpion is the dangerous resident of Bouhedma's sandy south, its thick metasoma as heavy as the rest of its body. It digs a shallow burrow at a bush base and ambushes passing beetles after dark.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The common yellow scorpion is the one most often encountered in Bouhedma's camps and stone walls. Like all scorpions it glows bright green-blue under ultraviolet light, a trick used by rangers to survey the park's population.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The Tunisian scorpion is the park's most widespread scorpion, sheltering by day under stones and in rodent burrows. Its sting is painful but rarely dangerous to a healthy adult, and it hunts beetles and other small invertebrates once the ground cools at night.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: The desert horned viper is the park's best-known venomous snake. It shuffles its body into the sand until only the eyes show, then waits for lizards and rodents to pass, moving off in a sidewinding ripple when disturbed.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The small sand viper lacks the horns of its cousin but shares its ambush tactics on the sandy flats of southern Bouhedma. Adults are among the smallest vipers in the region, rarely longer than a forearm, and vanish with a single wriggle.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The Montpellier snake is fast, alert and only mildly venomous to people, but deadly to mice and lizards. It rears its forebody into a tight S when cornered, showing the pale V on the back of its head.
source_reference: Park checklist (baseline survey)

description: The Algerian rat snake is a large, alert climber of rocky slopes, drystone walls and farm buildings — the most snake-like predator of Bouhedma's ruins. Fast and harmless to people, it hunts rodents, birds and lizards, and will take eggs if it finds them.
source_reference: iNaturalist - Bouhedma National Park Talent Academy

description: A heavy, boldly patterned viper of the low mountains and the cultivation edges, active from dusk to midnight. Its bite is medically important, so every encounter is reported to the park staff.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: A very slender, fast snake of the sands, olive or striped, that hunts lizards in daylight. It freezes against a bush first, then leaves in a straight rush that is easy to lose in the grass.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)

description: The land tortoise of the scrub, with a high domed shell and a spur on each thigh. It grazes on herbs in the cool hours, shelters under a bush at midday and buries its eggs in the sandy soil.
source_reference: Bouhedma species list — Guide to Codes, 3rd ed. (BHD26, 2026)
